📍 Brussels, Belgium | 🏢 Hybrid | 💼 Full-time
📅 Contract: ASAP – 12 Months
🎯 Target Date: 24/09/2026
🌐 Languages: Dutch + English + French
🔐 Are you experienced in Data Governance, Compliance and regulatory frameworks?

Join an enterprise-wide Data Governance function focused on strengthening governance, compliance, transparency and trust in data assets while bridging Business, IT, Security, Risk, Legal and Privacy teams.

Define and maintain the Data Governance roadmap
Ensure compliance with GDPR, EU Data Act, NIS2 & AI Act

Identify governance gaps/non-compliance and define corrective actions
Define data ownership, roles and governance bodies
Lead the Data Governance Community and chair the Governance Board
Drive governance-by-design and business process optimization
Develop training and promote data literacy
Define KPIs, monitor maturity, adoption and results
Represent Data Governance in strategic programs and steering committees

3–4 years’ experience in Data Governance, Data Management or IT Governance
Experience in regulated/complex organizations
Strong Business, IT, Architecture & Platform collaboration
Knowledge of data products, master data, data quality & compliance
Familiarity with GDPR, EU Data Act & AI Act
Strong stakeholder management, facilitation and communication skills
Analytical, structured, proactive and autonomous
Strong change management, coaching and community-building skills
Nice to have: Snowflake, dbt, AWS, data catalog, BI & data lifecycle management

WHEN ONE MARKET DRIVES YOUR REVENUE, TRADE POLICY CREATES BUSINESS RISK.

Closer Canada-EU cooperation has renewed the conversation about diversification. But for many Canadian businesses, the immediate question is not whether Europe offers opportunity. It is how prepared they are if conditions in the United States change.

I have worked in organizations where approximately 70% to 80% of revenue came from the U.S. That concentration supported growth, but it also meant that tariffs, currency movements, border delays and changing demand could quickly affect revenue, margins and cash flow.

The same risk exists in the supply chain. A tariff may force a company to change suppliers, renegotiate contracts, adjust prices or carry more inventory. Each response affects working capital and may introduce new quality, capacity or delivery risks.

Should a Canadian company pivot away from the U.S. or stop pursuing new business there? Not necessarily. The U.S. may remain its largest and most attractive market. But relying on one market without a practical alternative is a risk leaders should understand.

Before making a major decision, I would want to see the scenarios:
• What happens if U.S. revenue declines by 10% or 20%?
• Which customers, products and margins are most exposed?
• Which products depend on U.S. or Chinese suppliers?
• Can tariff and currency costs be passed to customers?
• When would we change suppliers, pricing, hiring or investment plans?
• How much cash would each response require?

This is not about predicting every policy decision. It is about deciding in advance what would trigger action.

📝 IntiEdge Field Note:
Concentration usually develops gradually. The largest market receives more investment, familiar suppliers receive more orders, and forecasts become increasingly dependent on both. That may feel efficient, until tariffs change, a supplier becomes uneconomic or customers begin delaying orders.

Finance can help leadership quantify the exposure, test the alternatives and protect cash flow before urgency narrows the available choices.
— Lessons from the field

💬 Question for leaders:
If conditions in your largest market changed tomorrow, would your leadership team know what to protect, what to pause and when to pivot?

💡 Friday Takeaway:
Diversification does not mean abandoning a successful market. It means building credible options before you need them.

Canada’s closer relationship with Europe may create new opportunities. But resilience begins with understanding current U.S. exposure and preparing realistic choices across customers, suppliers, pricing, hiring and cash flow.

If your organization is navigating these uncertainties and needs help turning exposure into financial scenarios and an actionable plan, let’s connect.

Everyone talks about framework design.

But real framework power comes from mastering OOP.

If you can’t explain OOP simply you don’t fully understand it.

Here are 12 OOP concepts every QA / SDET must know:
➩ Class – Blueprint of test design
➩ Object – Runtime instance (like WebDriver session)
➩ Interface – Contract enforcing structure
➩ Encapsulation – Protecting locators & logic
➩ Abstraction – Exposing essentials, hiding complexity
➩ Inheritance – Reusing common setup (avoid deep chains)
➩ Polymorphism – Same method, different behavior
➩ Association – Collaboration between classes
➩ Aggregation – Independent lifecycle relationship
➩ Composition – Strong ownership relationship
➩ Dependency – Temporary usage via parameters
➩ Realization – Implementing interface contract

Most frameworks don’t fail because of tools like Selenium or Playwright.
They fail because:
➩ OOP principles were ignored
➩ Responsibilities weren’t separated
➩ Tight coupling was introduced
➩ Design patterns were misused

If your framework is hard to scale, debug, or maintain, it’s likely a design problem, not a tool problem.

Before learning another tool, ask yourself:

The bigger lesson?

your onboarding is a person. that's the whole problem.
say you sell software to insurers or clinics or freight brokers. the product works, the demos land, the contracts get signed.
then the customer sends their data. a csv or a snowflake share if you're lucky. it's in their shape, not yours, with field names that meant something to somebody in that building long ago. so someone on your team spends two weeks working out what is what before the product does anything at all.
every customer. forever.
half the time it turns up as an excel export with merged header cells, which is its own separate punishment.
nobody puts this on a budget line because it's just what onboarding is. but it sets your ceiling. you cannot sign customers faster than one person can read, and hiring for it buys a cost that grows at the same rate as revenue. anaconda's survey put 45 percent of a data professional's day on preparation against about 11 percent on the modelling. gartner expects 60 percent of ai projects to be abandoned through 2026 where the data underneath them isn't ready.

Most engineers use REST APIs every day and then struggle to explain them in an interview.

Not because they do not know. Because nobody ever asked them to say it out loud.

So I wrote out what actually gets asked, and what the interviewer is listening for.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗢𝗣𝗘𝗡𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗤𝗨𝗘𝗦𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡

"How would you test this endpoint?" They are not asking for a list. They want to hear you pick an order. Contract, happy path, auth, bad input, edges. Saying "I would start with the contract" already puts you ahead of most people.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗖𝗢𝗗𝗘𝗦 𝗧𝗛𝗘𝗬 𝗔𝗖𝗧𝗨𝗔𝗟𝗟𝗬 𝗔𝗦𝗞 𝗔𝗕𝗢𝗨𝗧

Four, not forty. 201 with a Location header. 202 means queued, not done. 401 versus 403, which teams mix constantly. And 422, which RFC 9110 renamed to Unprocessable Content. The old name is from the WebDAV spec.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗣

202 means the work is queued. If your test asserts on the result straight after a 202, it is flaky forever and you will spend a month blaming the network.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗤𝗨𝗘𝗦𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗧𝗛𝗔𝗧 𝗦𝗢𝗥𝗧𝗦 𝗣𝗘𝗢𝗣𝗟𝗘

"Are you validating response bodies, or just status codes?" A 200 with a null where the user ID should be is a passing test and a broken integration.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗢𝗡𝗘 𝗠𝗢𝗦𝗧 𝗣𝗘𝗢𝗣𝗟𝗘 𝗚𝗘𝗧 𝗪𝗥𝗢𝗡𝗚

Per RFC 9110, GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT and DELETE are idempotent. POST and PATCH are not. PATCH gets called idempotent constantly and it is not. If a client times out, retries, and creates a second order, that is not a network bug.

Seven pages of notes, all of it from questions I have actually asked or been asked.

Oracle laid off workers and refused to negotiate severance. Some discovered they didn't qualify for WARN Act protections because Oracle classified them as remote.

This matters to you because it exposes a compliance gap most founders don't see coming.

Here's what happened: Remote workers in the US are supposed to get 60 days' notice under the WARN Act if a company cuts 50+ employees at a single site. Oracle's argument? Remote workers aren't at a "site," so the rule doesn't apply. The workers disagreed. Oracle said no to better terms anyway.

Why this is your problem:

1. **Classification risk**: If you're scaling ops across LATAM or Israel and hiring remote workers, how are you documenting their work location for labor compliance? One misclassification and you're exposed.

2. **Severance negotiation leverage**: Your team assumes they have legal protections. They might not. When layoffs happen (and they do), you need to know what you actually owe before employees find out you don't.

3. **Automation won't save you**: You can't automate away labor law. But you can automate the *tracking* - employee location, contract terms, notice period obligations. Most founders skip this until it costs them.

4. **LATAM + Israel context**: Severance laws in these regions are stricter than the US. If you're hiring across borders, you need a system that flags compliance gaps before they become disputes.

The fix: Audit your employee classification system now. Remote doesn't mean unclassified. Build a simple n8n workflow or spreadsheet that tracks: location, contract type, notice period owed, severance formula. Run it quarterly.

Oracle's workers learned the hard way that "no" is a valid answer when you haven't documented what you actually owe.

Don't be Oracle.

I'm sitting at breakfast at the Marcliffe this morning, thinking about my home in Aberdeen.

I arrived in 1976, a young recruiter from London, and set up my first business just as the North Sea oil boom was beginning. I had no idea what this place was about to become. 
But you could feel it. Oil flowing. International companies arriving. Offices opening. People coming from all over the world. Projects to staff, engineers to find, businesses to build.

Fifty years later, I'm getting that feeling again.

Take where I'm sitting. 

The Marcliffe is now owned by Balmoral Group, the Aberdeen company Sir Jim Milne founded. 
They're investing more than £50 million across their businesses and new opportunities, and establishing a new Aberdeen headquarters.

Drive down to the Port of Aberdeen. The £420 million South Harbour has changed what the port can handle. 

Oil and gas vessels come and go, but so do offshore wind vessels  around 700 calls a year now. 

National Gas is putting another £55 million into its Aberdeen Compressor Station. 

Well Safe Solutions is building around the enormous decommissioning market, covering hundreds of wells. 

And new industries are appearing.

Maybe Aberdeen isn't finished. Maybe it's changing again.

And that brings me back to recruitment.

After 50 years, I look at every one of those stories and think: where are the jobs? Not the ones advertised today. The ones coming next.

That's why I'm launching CrewDog AI  a predictive job board. Instead of waiting for a vacancy to appear, it looks for the things that happen before companies start hiring. 

A contract awarded. CAPEX approved. A rig gets a programme. A project reaches FID. A company expands. A decommissioning campaign starts.

Then you ask CrewDog: what happens next? What skills will they need? When might they need them? Who should I be talking to now?

It's simply what good recruiters have always done, given AI. Discover the job before it becomes a job advert.

I'm also building CrewDog TV. That's the bit I want to have some fun with. I'm forever filming around Aberdeen ,vessels in harbour, new businesses, projects, events, entrepreneurs. So I'm using it to promote Aberdeen companies and tell some of those stories.



CrewDog TV asks: who is building Aberdeen and what’s it like today.

CrewDog AI asks: where will that create jobs?

I started recruiting when we needed people to drill the wells. 
Now I'm helping find people to plug and abandon them. From drilling to decommissioning, I've been in this game from cradle to grave.

I'm 75 now. Perhaps I should be looking backwards.

I'm not.

Fifty years after starting my first business in Aberdeen, I'm starting again.

Different technology. 

Same Aberdeen. Same fun.

And I'm still in the game.
 
If your business is in Aberdeen or your looking to expand here I would like to share your videos on CrewDog TV

Federal aviation officials are preparing to launch an AI-powered air-traffic tool in one of the nation’s busiest corridors as soon as Monday.

The software, known as Smart, is expected to help the Federal Aviation Administration and airlines reduce delays and cancellations and find routes for flights when disruptions scramble air traffic. It will first debut in the Washington, D.C., area ahead of a broader nationwide rollout, according to government and industry officials.

Smart stands for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories. The software has the ability to analyze airline schedules and factors such as weather, airport runway capacity and operational constraints to predict air-traffic flows and identify potential conflicts before they occur.  

When fully rolled out across U.S. airspace, the software is supposed to act as something like the brains of the nation’s air-traffic control system. The firm Air Space Intelligence won a $875 million, 12-year government contract earlier this year to build out Smart and a related system.

The Trump administration has directed billions of dollars to upgrade the nation’s aging air-traffic infrastructure with new technology. The administration has also been trying to ramp up hiring and training of air-traffic controllers. Staffing shortages at air-traffic facilities are frequent sources of disruptions.

FAA officials have been discussing with airlines how to coordinate their schedules as part of the software’s broader rollout. Industry officials have had questions about how the system would work, particularly given carriers’ fierce competition to operate flights at certain times of day.

“The way we manage traffic today is chaotic, and we can do better,” FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford, a former regional airline executive, said during Senate testimony earlier this year. “We need to manage that at the FAA, rather than rely on commercial airlines to simply schedule however they want.”

🌍 How to Land a Remote Job From Anywhere in the World Without Local Connections
You don't need family connections, a local network, or an office in another country to start pursuing remote work. What you need is a useful skill, proof that you can deliver results, and a reliable way to reach employers or clients.
🚀 1. Pick One Remote-Friendly Skill
Don't try to learn everything at once. Focus on one marketable skill:
https://lnkd.in/ea-UM4kx
https://lnkd.in/eqsc9hNY
https://lnkd.in/ejvzxWiS
👉 **GET THE EBOOK HERE:**
[Social Media Jobs That Pay Well] https://lnkd.in/eZqjZPNd or https://lnkd.in/ebFzZYR6
👉 **EXPLORE MORE EBOOKS & DIGITAL PRODUCTS:**
[King Collins Ya on Selar] https://lnkd.in/eZqjZPNd or https://lnkd.in/ebFzZYR6
✍️ Copywriting
🎨 Graphic design
🎬 Video editing
💻 Web development
🤖 AI automation
📱 Social media management
📊 Data analysis
🧑‍🏫 Online tutoring
🎧 Customer support
🧩 2. Build Proof Before You Apply
No experience? Create your own experience.
Build 3–5 sample projects that demonstrate what you can do.
For example, if you want to become a social media manager, create a sample content calendar, design several posts, and explain how you would grow a fictional brand.
Your portfolio can often communicate your abilities better than simply saying, “I have experience.”
🌐 3. Search Beyond Your Local Job Market
Look for companies that explicitly hire internationally or advertise remote worldwide positions.
Useful places to search include:
LinkedIn
Wellfound
Remote OK
We Work Remotely
Upwork
Contra
FlexJobs
Always check the job's geographic restrictions. “Remote” does not necessarily mean “work from anywhere.” Some employers require workers to live in a particular country, region, or time zone.
💬 4. Don't Rely Only on Job Applications
You can also contact companies directly.
Find businesses that could benefit from your skill, research the person responsible for hiring or the relevant department, and send a short message explaining:
Problem → What you can do → Proof → Simple next step
Avoid sending the same generic message to hundreds of companies.
💵 5. Start With Smaller Projects
Your first objective doesn't have to be a six-figure remote job.
A small freelance project can give you:
Experience → Portfolio → Testimonial → Credibility → Better opportunities
Once you have evidence of your results, you can target larger clients and higher-paying positions.
🌍 6. Make Yourself Easy to Hire Internationally
Have these ready:
✅ Professional CV
✅ Portfolio
✅ LinkedIn profile
✅ Reliable internet
✅ Professional communication
✅ Suitable payment method
✅ Availability/time zone
✅ Clear description of your services
Also understand how the employer handles international employment, contracts, taxes, and payments.
